candidates.quote: I want to be useful or bring enjoyment to all people, even those I’ve never met.
candidates.author: Anne Frank
candidates.work: The Diary of a Young Girl
candidates.locator: the entry of 5 April 1944 (the Definitive Edition, Doubleday, 1995)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A girl with almost nothing to give works out at fourteen that usefulness is what she wants, and the wish reaches a reader before the day has asked anything of them.

candidates.quote: You have not done enough, you have never done enough, so long as it is still possible that you have something of value to contribute.
candidates.author: Dag Hammarskjöld
candidates.translator: Leif Sjöberg and W. H. Auden, 1964
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence for a morning when the ledger feels settled: it is not settled, while you still have something to give.

candidates.quote: In Louisville, at the corner of Fourth and Walnut, in the center of the shopping district, I was suddenly overwhelmed with the realization that I loved all those people, that they were mine and I theirs, that we could not be alien to one another even though we were total strangers.
candidates.author: Thomas Merton
candidates.locator: Part Three, The Night Spirit and the Dawn Air (Doubleday, 1966)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man who had spent years apart from people steps into a shopping street and finds he belongs to them, which is the month’s argument standing on one street corner.

candidates.quote: I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors.
candidates.author: Abigail Adams
candidates.locator: Braintree, 31 March to 5 April 1776 (Adams Family Correspondence, Massachusetts Historical Society)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The politest revolutionary sentence in English, and a reminder at six that justice is usually asked for by somebody who has to ask twice.

candidates.quote: Human beings have rights, because they are moral beings: the rights of all men grow out of their moral nature; and as all men have the same moral nature, they have essentially the same rights.
candidates.author: Angelina Grimké
candidates.locator: Letter XII, Human Rights Not Founded on Sex, 2 October 1837 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The ground under the whole month set out in one sentence: rights are owed for what people are, not for what they are called.

candidates.quote: Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.
candidates.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
candidates.locator: the letter of 16 April 1963, printed in Why We Can’t Wait (Harper and Row, 1964)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The line that makes distance irrelevant before breakfast: what is done to anyone is being done inside the garment you are wearing.

candidates.quote: Most that I have done and suffered in the service of our cause has been in public, and I have received much encouragement at every step of the way. You on the other hand have labored in a private way.
candidates.author: Frederick Douglass
candidates.locator: Rochester, 29 August 1868, printed in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman, p. 6 (1869)
candidates.whyThisMonth: For every reader whose work is unwitnessed, the most applauded man in the country says plainly that the private labour was the harder of the two.

candidates.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
candidates.author: Charles Dickens
candidates.locator: Stave One, Marley’s Ghost (Chapman and Hall, 1843)
candidates.speaker: the Ghost of Jacob Marley
candidates.whyThisMonth: A ghost says the thing any working morning needs to hear: the trade was never the business, the common welfare was.

candidates.quote: But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.
candidates.author: George Eliot
candidates.locator: the Finale, the closing sentence (William Blackwood and Sons, 1871 to 1872)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The novel’s last breath, and the best answer there is to waking up ordinary: the good of the world rests on acts nobody will record.

candidates.quote: Fellowship is life, and lack of fellowship is death: and the deeds that ye do upon the earth, it is for fellowship’s sake that ye do them.
candidates.author: William Morris
candidates.locator: chapter IV, The Voice of John Ball (Reeves and Turner, 1888)
candidates.speaker: John Ball
candidates.whyThisMonth: Preached at a crossroads in a dream of 1381, and still the plainest account of why any of this is owed: the fellowship is the life.

candidates.quote: When we gather together in the moonlit village ground it is not because of the moon. Every man can see it in his own compound. We come together because it is good for kinsmen to do so.
candidates.author: Chinua Achebe
candidates.speaker: one of the oldest members of the umunna
candidates.whyThisMonth: An old man explains why people gather when nothing at all requires it, which is the quiet half of what is owed.

candidates.quote: We know that there is no help for us but from one another, that no hand will save us if we do not reach out our hand.
candidates.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
candidates.locator: chapter 9, Shevek’s speech in Nio Esseia (Harper and Row, 1974)
candidates.speaker: Shevek
candidates.whyThisMonth: Given to a man speaking with empty hands, and it arrives as the morning’s practical instruction: put the hand out.

candidates.quote: I sit on a man’s back, choking him and making him carry me, and yet assure myself and others that I am very sorry for him and wish to ease his lot by all possible means—except by getting off his back.
candidates.author: Leo Tolstoy
candidates.locator: chapter XVI (trans. Aylmer Maude, Oxford World’s Classics, 1925)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most uncomfortable sentence ever written about charity, and the one worth meeting early, while the day can still be changed.

candidates.quote: Why have women passion, intellect, moral activity—these three—and a place in society where no one of the three can be exercised?
candidates.author: Florence Nightingale
candidates.locator: p. 74 (Cassandra: An Essay, The Feminist Press, 1979)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written by a woman with everything in her and nothing to do, it turns the month’s question outward: who near you is being wasted?

candidates.quote: As a woman, I have no country. As a woman I want no country. As a woman my country is the whole world.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.speaker: the outsider
candidates.whyThisMonth: For a morning when loyalty is being demanded of you, the widest answer available, given quietly.

candidates.quote: The notion of obligations comes before that of rights, which is subordinate and relative to the former.
candidates.author: Simone Weil
candidates.locator: Part One, The Needs of the Soul, the opening sentence (trans. Arthur Wills, 1952)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence that puts the month in order: before anything at all is claimed, something is owed.
